passages.t: Not at any time, and not in any way
passages.happening:
“Now the LORD spoke to Moses after the death of two of Aaron’s sons when they approached the presence of the LORD” (verse 1).

He says, “Tell your brother Aaron not to enter freely into the Most Holy Place behind the veil in front of the mercy seat on the ark, or else he will die, because I appear in the cloud above the mercy seat” (verse 2).

Aaron is to come with a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering (verse 3). “He is to wear the sacred linen tunic, with linen undergarments”, a linen sash and a linen turban, and he must bathe before he puts them on (verse 4). From the people he takes two male goats and a ram (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The chapter begins by looking back to chapter 10, where Nadab and Abihu came near to God in a way he had not commanded, and died. That day left a question hanging. How can anyone come close to a holy God and live? Chapters 11 to 15 dealt with the uncleanness of everyday life. This chapter gathers up everything those laws could not reach, the uncleanness and the rebellion of a whole year, and deals with it in one great cleansing.

It stands at the center of the book. It is the hinge between the laws about purity before it and the call to holy living after it.

A first reader pictured the tent as a house with rooms of rising holiness. Outside was the courtyard with its altar. Inside was the Holy Place, where priests served every day. Behind a thick woven curtain was the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant stood. God's presence appeared above the ark's gold lid, the mercy seat. No one went into that room but the high priest, and he went only on this day.

Notice what he wore. On other days the high priest was dressed in gold and jewels. On this day he bathed and put on plain white linen. It was closer to a servant's dress. He came before God without his splendor.

And notice the first word spoken to Aaron in this chapter. It is a warning, but it is also a way. God does not say that Aaron may never come in. He says how he may.
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews describes this day: “only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance” (Hebrews 9:7).

It also says what the curtain meant, and what Christians believe has changed: “we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:19-20).
passages.asks: The high priest came on God's terms, washed, and without his splendor. Ask what you bring with you when you come to God that you are proud of, and what it would mean to leave it at the door. And ask whether you hear God's conditions for coming near as a wall or as a way in.

passages.t: A bull for himself, and two goats
passages.happening:
“Aaron is to present the bull for his sin offering and make atonement for himself and his household” (verse 6).

Then he takes the two goats and sets them before the LORD at the entrance to the tent. He “casts lots for the two goats, one for the LORD and the other for the scapegoat” (verse 8). The goat on which the lot for the LORD falls is to be sacrificed as a sin offering (verse 9).

“But the goat chosen by lot as the scapegoat shall be presented alive before the LORD to make atonement by sending it into the wilderness as the scapegoat” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
These verses give a short summary of the day before the chapter walks through it slowly. That is why the bull and the goats are named twice.

The high priest begins with himself. Before he can stand for the people, atonement has to be made for him and his family.

Then come two goats. A lot decides between them. Casting lots was a way of leaving a choice to God. So it is God, not the priest, who chooses which goat dies and which is sent away.

The day needs both. One goat's blood will be carried inward, to cleanse the holy place. The other goat will carry the people's sins outward, away from the camp. A reader who merges the two goats into one loses the point of the chapter.

Where the Berean Standard Bible says ‘scapegoat’, the Hebrew has a name or word, Azazel, which occurs only in this chapter. Its meaning is uncertain, and the hard question below sets out the readings.
passages.later:
The Bible speaks elsewhere of the lot as a way God decides: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

The pattern of two creatures, one killed and one set free, has already appeared once in this book, in the two birds used when a person healed of skin disease was brought home (Leviticus 14:4-7).
passages.hard:
Who or what is Azazel? Was the goat sent to a demon?

The question is fair. Verse 8 sets ‘for the LORD’ beside the other goat's lot in the same form, which may suggest that Azazel is a name. A Jewish book from a few centuries before Jesus, 1 Enoch, uses Azazel as the name of a fallen angel bound in the desert. The next chapter forbids Israel to sacrifice to ‘goat demons’ (17:7), so such beliefs were known. Many modern scholars, Jacob Milgrom among them, think Azazel was at first the name of a spirit of the wilderness.

Others read the word differently. The old Greek and Latin translations took it as a description of the goat: the one sent away. William Tyndale followed them in 1530 and coined the English word ‘scapegoat’. The Talmud and the medieval Jewish commentator Rashi took Azazel as the name of a hard, rocky place. Others read it as a word for complete removal.

On every reading the chapter's own teaching is clear. Only the LORD receives sacrifice. The goat for Azazel is not killed, and nothing is offered to anyone but God. The lots are cast before the LORD. Milgrom himself argued that whatever the word once meant, Leviticus has emptied it of power. The goat's task is to carry Israel's confessed sins away from the camp, to the waste places where they belong.

Which reading of the word is right remains open, and careful interpreters hold each of them.
passages.asks: God chose which goat would die and which would go free. Ask whether you trust God with outcomes you cannot control. And think about the two movements of the day, cleansing within and sin carried away. Ask which you find harder to believe: that God can make you clean, or that what you have confessed is truly gone.

passages.happening:
Aaron kills the bull for his own sin offering (verse 11). He takes a pan of burning coals from the altar and two handfuls of fine incense inside the veil. “He is to put the incense on the fire before the LORD, and the cloud of incense will cover the mercy seat above the Testimony, so that he will not die” (verse 13). He sprinkles the bull's blood on the mercy seat and seven times in front of it (verse 14).

Then he kills the goat for the people's sin offering, brings its blood behind the veil, and does the same (verse 15). “So he shall make atonement for the Most Holy Place because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (verse 16). He does the same for the Tent of Meeting, and then for the altar outside (verses 16-19).

No one else may be in the tent while he is inside (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
This is the center of the day, and no one saw it but the high priest. He was alone in the tent.

He went in with smoke before him. The cloud of incense hid the mercy seat, so that he did not look straight at the place where God appeared. The coals came from the altar, as God had laid down. Nadab and Abihu had brought fire of their own.

The mercy seat is, in Hebrew, the kapporet. The word shares its root with kipper, to make atonement. It was the gold cover of the ark, with two winged figures above it. Blood was sprinkled there, at the place of God's presence.

Why does a place need atonement? The chapter assumes that sin and uncleanness do not stay with the person. They stain the place where God lives, as smoke stains a house. Over a year the tent had been ‘surrounded by their impurities’. Now it is cleansed, room by room, from the inside out: the Most Holy Place, then the tent, then the altar.

Two words in verse 16 are worth noticing. ‘Impurities’ are the uncleanness of ordinary life, which is not sin. ‘Rebellious acts’ are deliberate wrongs, the kind the ordinary sin offerings of chapter 4 did not cover. This day reaches both.

The verb ‘make atonement’ comes sixteen times in this chapter.
passages.later:
Paul uses this chapter's word of Jesus. “God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood” (Romans 3:25). The Greek word there is the one the old Greek translation used for the mercy seat.

Hebrews says that Christ “did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God” (Hebrews 9:24).

Matthew records that when Jesus died, “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51).

These lines are drawn by the New Testament itself. They do not make Israel's worship empty. As the notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real, and God truly met his people and forgave them here.
passages.asks: Sin in this chapter stains more than the person who commits it. Ask where you have seen a wrong spread beyond the one who did it, into a family, a church or a workplace. And ask what in your own shared life, at home or among God's people, needs cleansing and not only your private conscience.

passages.t: The goat that carries sins away
passages.happening:
“When Aaron has finished purifying the Most Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar, he is to bring forward the live goat” (verse 20).

“Then he is to lay both hands on the head of the live goat and confess over it all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins. He is to put them on the goat’s head and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man appointed for the task” (verse 21).

“The goat will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place, and the man will release it into the wilderness” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Now the people could watch. What happened behind the curtain was hidden. This was done in front of everyone.

In the ordinary offerings a worshiper pressed one hand on the animal's head. Here the high priest uses both hands, and he speaks. He says aloud the sins of the people. The verse piles up the words for wrong as nowhere else in Leviticus: iniquities, rebellious acts, sins. Nothing is left out. And it says what the gesture means: he puts them ‘on the goat’s head’.

Then a man leads the goat out of the camp, further and further, into the wilderness, the empty land beyond the ordered world of the camp. The Hebrew for ‘a solitary place’ means a land cut off. The goat does not come back.

It is a picture a child could understand, and that is its strength. The people's sins have been named, laid on another, and taken away to a place from which they do not return.

Israel's neighbors had rites that look alike from a distance. Texts from Ebla in Syria and from the Hittites tell of an animal driven out to carry away sickness or evil. Leviticus shares the idea that what defiles can be carried off. But here there are no spells and no spirits to be bought off. Everything is done because the LORD commanded it. And the goat carries confessed sin, not disease.
passages.later:
A psalm sings of sin taken as far as can be imagined: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).

The prophet Micah says to God, “You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19).

Isaiah writes of the servant of the LORD, “the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). The New Testament does not say in so many words that this goat is a picture of Christ, but Christians have long seen in it a picture of sin carried away, as when John the Baptist said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). That link is one of likeness and should be held as such.
passages.hard:
How could a goat sent into the desert, or the blood of animals, really deal with human guilt?

The question is old. The New Testament asks it of itself: “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). Philosophers have pressed it too. Guilt, they say, is the most personal of debts. It cannot be handed to another as a debt of money can. On that view, laying sin on a goat confuses moral guilt with dirt, and the rite is a kind of magic.

Jewish and Christian readers both answer that it was never magic. Jewish teachers have long held that the rite did nothing apart from repentance. The people fasted and humbled themselves. The Mishnah teaches that repentance atones together with the day, and that a wrong done to a neighbor is not covered until it has been put right with the neighbor. Christian readers agree that the animals had no power in themselves. The blood atones, Leviticus says, because God has given it for that purpose (17:11). Scholars such as Jacob Milgrom stress that the day is about cleansing the sanctuary so that God can stay among his people. It is not a bribe.

From there the two readings part. On the Christian reading, the Day of Atonement was God's real provision for Israel in its time, and also a picture pointing ahead to a sacrifice that could do fully what the yearly rite could only show. Hebrews says that Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself” (Hebrews 9:26). Many Jewish readers see the rite as complete in its own terms. Since the temple was destroyed in AD 70, they have kept the day through prayer, fasting and repentance.

This day is Yom Kippur, still the holiest day of the Jewish year. In the synagogue this chapter is read on its morning, and the service retells the high priest's work in the temple. Christians should speak of this living observance with respect, and never as empty or merely a matter of rules. Its insistence that a person must first make peace with a neighbor is a searching word to Christian readers too.

The disagreement between the two readings is real. A reader can see that both take seriously what the chapter claims: that God himself provides the way back.
passages.asks: The sins were named aloud, laid on the goat, and led away where they could not return. Ask what wrong of yours you have confessed many times and still carry. And ask what it would mean to believe that God has taken it as far as the east is from the west.

passages.t: Washing, and burning outside the camp
passages.happening:
Aaron goes back into the tent, takes off the linen garments and leaves them there (verse 23). He bathes in a holy place, puts on his own garments, and offers the two burnt offerings, his own and the people's (verse 24). He burns the fat of the sin offering on the altar (verse 25).

“The man who released the goat as the scapegoat must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp” (verse 26).

The bull and the goat “whose blood was brought into the Most Holy Place to make atonement, must be taken outside the camp”, and burned (verse 27). The man who burns them washes too (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The day ends as carefully as it began. Everything that has touched the work of the day is dealt with.

The plain linen is left behind in the tent. It was for that room and that hour. The high priest washes again and puts on his usual garments.

Then come the burnt offerings, the whole gifts of chapter 1. Cleansing is followed by the giving of oneself to God, in the same order as on the priests' first day (chapter 9).

The two men who handled what carried sin away, the one who led the goat and the one who burned the bodies, wash before they come back into the camp. The holy and the unclean are kept apart to the last.

The bodies of the two sin offerings are not eaten. Their blood went into the innermost room, and such offerings are burned outside the camp (6:30).
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews draws on verse 27: “the bodies are burned outside the camp. And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (Hebrews 13:11-12).

It then turns the place of shame into a call: “Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore” (Hebrews 13:13).
passages.asks: The man who led the goat away did a lonely, unclean task so that others could be clean. Ask who does hard and unseen work for the good of your community. And ask whether you are willing to go ‘outside the camp’, to places and people others avoid, when faithfulness asks it.

passages.t: A day for all the people, every year
passages.happening:
“This is to be a permanent statute for you: On the tenth day of the seventh month, you shall humble yourselves and not do any work” (verse 29). It applies to the native-born and to the foreigner living among them.

The reason follows: “because on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (verse 30). “It is a Sabbath of complete rest for you, that you may humble yourselves; it is a permanent statute” (verse 31).

Each new high priest is to do the same after his father (verses 32-33). It is to be done “once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins” (verse 34). “And all this was done as the LORD had commanded Moses” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The last paragraph turns from the priest to the people. They do not go behind the curtain. But the day is theirs.

They have two things to do. They are to ‘humble yourselves’, which Israel understood as fasting. It was the one fast required by the law of Moses. And they are to do no work at all.

That second thing matters. The people do not earn their cleansing. The high priest does the work, and atonement is ‘made for you’. The people receive it at rest. The Hebrew phrase for ‘a Sabbath of complete rest’ is used only of the weekly Sabbath and of this day. That is why Jewish tradition calls Yom Kippur the Sabbath of Sabbaths.

The promise of verse 30 is as wide as the confession of verse 21: ‘clean from all your sins’.

The foreigner living among Israel is included. And the words ‘a permanent statute’ come three times. This was to be kept every year.

The chapter ends where it began, with Moses, Aaron and God's command. But the ending turns the opening round. Aaron's sons died doing what the LORD had not commanded. The last line says that all this was done as he commanded.
passages.later:
The feast calendar repeats the day: “The tenth day of this seventh month is the Day of Atonement. You shall hold a sacred assembly and humble yourselves” (Leviticus 23:27).

Isaiah warned that a fast means nothing if it leaves injustice alone: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free” (Isaiah 58:6). In the synagogue this part of Isaiah is read on Yom Kippur.

The book of Acts dates a sea voyage by this day and calls it simply ‘the Fast’ (Acts 27:9).

Hebrews takes the yearly repeating as a sign that the day pointed beyond itself: “those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins” (Hebrews 10:3). Of Christ it says, “when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12).
passages.asks: The people were made clean while they rested and someone else worked for them. Ask whether you try to earn God's forgiveness by effort, or by punishing yourself. And ask what it would mean, today, to stop, to be honest about your sins, and to receive a cleansing you did not achieve.
